learn.hook: Pull out a mustard seedling and a wheat seedling from a Punjab field. One has a single deep anchor; the other has a bushy beard of roots.
points: Morphology is the study of the external form and features of organisms. A flowering plant has a root, stem, leaves, flowers and fruits.
Tap root system: in most dicots the radicle elongates into a primary root that bears secondary and tertiary lateral roots, e.g. mustard.
Fibrous root system: in monocots the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by many roots arising from the base of the stem, e.g. wheat.
Adventitious roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle, e.g. grass, Monstera and the banyan tree.
Functions of roots: absorption of water and minerals, anchorage, storage of reserve food, and synthesis of plant growth regulators.

example.q: A banyan's hanging roots grow down from its branches. Classify these roots and explain.
steps: Tap and fibrous roots develop from the radicle or stem base of a seedling.
These roots arise from branches, a part other than the radicle.

learn.reallife: The banyan, India's national tree, spreads using adventitious roots that become pillar-like; the Great Banyan in Howrah's botanical garden covers several acres.

games.title: Root system
items: Primary root from radicle with laterals
Many roots from stem base in monocots

games.title: Root facts
items: Tap roots develop from the radicle.
Direct elongation of the radicle forms the primary root.
Monocots usually have a tap root system.
Roots can synthesise plant growth regulators.
This is one of their functions.
Adventitious roots arise only from the radicle.
They arise from parts other than the radicle.
Morphology studies the external form of plants.

quiz.q: The tap root system develops from the:
quiz.explain: The radicle elongates directly into the primary root.

quiz.q: Wheat has which type of root system?
quiz.explain: Monocots like wheat have fibrous roots from the stem base.

quiz.q: Roots arising from any part of the plant other than the radicle are called:
quiz.explain: Adventitious roots arise from stem, branches or nodes.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a function of roots?
quiz.explain: Leaves are the main photosynthetic organs; roots absorb, anchor, store and make growth regulators.
options: Photosynthesis as the main food-making organ

quiz.q: Morphology is the study of:
quiz.explain: Anatomy studies internal structure; morphology studies external form.

quiz.q: In monocots, the primary root is:
quiz.explain: This replacement forms the fibrous root system.
quiz.mistake: Thinks monocots keep their primary root
options: Short-lived and replaced by many roots from the stem base

quiz.q: Mustard is an example of a plant with:
quiz.explain: Mustard is a dicot with a tap root.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up dicot and monocot roots

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Banyan has adventitious roots. Reason (R): In the banyan, roots grow down from the branches.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; roots from branches arise from a part other than the radicle, so they are adventitious.
quiz.mistake: Misses that the origin defines adventitious roots

teach.ask: Gappu pulls up mustard and wheat seedlings. 'Why do their roots look so different?' Explain root systems to him!
teach.praise: Tweet! Tap for mustard, fibrous for wheat, adventitious for banyan. Rooted in facts!
teach.nudge: Good! Where does each root system come from?

topics.title: Regions of the root, and the stem

learn.hook: A root tip pushes through hard soil every day without getting hurt. It wears a helmet, just like a cricketer facing a fast bowler.
points: The root apex is covered by a thimble-like root cap that protects it as it pushes through soil.
Region of meristematic activity, a few millimetres above the root cap: small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide repeatedly.

Region of elongation: cells elongate and enlarge rapidly, making the root grow in length. Region of maturation: cells differentiate; some epidermal cells form fine root hairs that absorb water and minerals.

The stem is the ascending part of the axis that develops from the plumule. It bears nodes (where leaves arise), internodes (between nodes), and terminal or axillary buds. It is green when young, often woody and dark brown later.
Stem functions: spreading out branches with leaves, flowers and fruits; conducting water, minerals and photosynthates; and in some plants storage, support, protection and vegetative propagation.

example.q: List the regions of a root from the tip upwards.
steps: Tip is covered by the root cap.
Next is the region of meristematic activity.
Then the region of elongation.
Then the region of maturation, which bears root hairs.
example.answer: Root cap → meristematic region → elongation region → maturation region

learn.reallife: Sugarcane growers in Uttar Pradesh plant stem cuttings with nodes to raise new plants, using the stem's power of vegetative propagation.

games.title: Regions of the root
items: Region of maturation with root hairs

items.text: The stem develops from the ___ of the embryo.
The part of a stem where leaves arise is a ___.
Root hairs arise in the region of ___.
Growth of a root in length is due to the region of ___.

quiz.q: Which part protects the tender root apex?
quiz.explain: The thimble-like root cap shields the apex.
quiz.mistake: Thinks root hairs protect the tip

quiz.q: Root hairs develop from the region of:
quiz.explain: Epidermal cells in the maturation region form root hairs.
quiz.mistake: Places root hairs in the elongation zone

quiz.q: Cells that divide repeatedly in a root lie in the:
quiz.explain: Small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm divide repeatedly there.

quiz.q: The portion of a stem between two nodes is the:
quiz.explain: Nodes bear leaves; internodes lie between nodes.

quiz.q: Which is a function of the stem?
quiz.explain: Stems conduct materials and spread branches.
options: Absorbing water from soil through root hairs

quiz.q: The stem develops from the:
quiz.explain: The plumule gives the shoot; the radicle gives the root.

quiz.q: Root hairs mainly:
quiz.explain: Their large surface area aids absorption.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A root grows in length mainly because of the root cap. Reason (R): Cells in the region of elongation enlarge and elongate rapidly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the root cap only protects the tip. R is true: rapid enlargement and elongation of cells in the region of elongation is what increases root length.
quiz.mistake: Judges the assertion true just because the reason is a correct fact

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw a root tip and a stem. Explain the root regions and the stem parts to him!
teach.praise: Chirp! Cap, meristem, elongation, maturation, then nodes and internodes up top. Perfect sketch!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the four regions of the root tip?

learn.hook: Watch a peepal leaf flutter in the slightest breeze. Its long, flexible petiole is cooling the leaf, a design trick worth learning.
points: A leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem at a node, with a bud in its axil. Leaves arise from the shoot apical meristem in acropetal order.

A typical leaf has a leaf base, petiole and lamina. The leaf base may bear two small leaf-like stipules. In monocots the leaf base forms a sheath around the stem; in some legumes it is swollen into a pulvinus.
The petiole holds the blade to the light. Long, thin, flexible petioles let blades flutter, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface.
The lamina is the green expanded part with veins and veinlets; the prominent middle vein is the midrib. Veins give rigidity and carry water, minerals and food.
Venation: reticulate (veinlets form a network), generally in dicots; parallel (veins run parallel), generally in monocots.

example.q: A leaf has parallel veins and a sheathing leaf base. What group does the plant probably belong to?
steps: Parallel venation is typical of monocots.
A sheathing leaf base is also a monocot feature.

learn.reallife: Banana and maize leaves show parallel venation, while the mango and peepal leaves used in Indian festive decorations show reticulate venation.

games.title: Leaf part to description
pairs: Attaches the leaf to the stem
Small leaf-like outgrowths at the base
Swollen leaf base in some legumes
Holds the blade to the light

quiz.q: A swollen leaf base in some leguminous plants is called the:
quiz.explain: The pulvinus is a swollen leaf base.

quiz.q: Venation in which veinlets form a network is:
quiz.explain: A network of veinlets is reticulate venation.

quiz.q: Parallel venation is typical of:
quiz.explain: Monocots generally have parallel venation.

quiz.q: How does a long flexible petiole help a leaf?
quiz.explain: Fluttering cools the leaf and refreshes air at its surface.
options: Lets the blade flutter, cooling it and bringing fresh air

quiz.q: The three main parts of a typical leaf are:
quiz.explain: Leaf base, petiole and lamina make a typical leaf.

quiz.q: In monocots, the leaf base usually:
quiz.explain: The sheathing leaf base is a monocot feature.
options: Expands into a sheath that covers the stem

quiz.q: Veins in the lamina:
quiz.explain: Veins support the blade and act as channels of transport.
options: Provide rigidity and transport water, minerals and food
Make the leaf fall in winter

quiz.q: Stipules are:
quiz.explain: Stipules are lateral outgrowths of the leaf base.
quiz.mistake: Confuses stipules with pulvinus or midrib
options: The swollen leaf base of legumes
Two small leaf-like structures that may be borne at the leaf base
The leaflets of a compound leaf

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how a leaf is built. Explain its parts and the two types of venation!
teach.praise: Tweet! Base, petiole, lamina, and nets for dicots, parallel lines for monocots!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the parts of a leaf, and what kinds of venation are there?

topics.title: Simple and compound leaves, and phyllotaxy

learn.hook: Is a neem 'leaf' one leaf or many? The answer depends on where you find a bud.
points: Simple leaf: the lamina is entire, or its incisions do not reach the midrib.
Compound leaf: incisions reach the midrib, breaking the lamina into leaflets. A bud is present in the axil of the petiole, but never in the axil of a leaflet.

Pinnately compound: leaflets on a common axis, the rachis (which represents the midrib), e.g. neem. Palmately compound: leaflets attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole, e.g. silk cotton.
Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem.
Alternate: one leaf per node (china rose, mustard, sunflower). Opposite: a pair of leaves per node, facing each other (Calotropis, guava). Whorled: more than two leaves per node (Alstonia).

example.q: How can you tell a leaflet of neem from a simple leaf?
steps: A simple leaf has a bud in its axil.
In a compound leaf, the bud is only in the axil of the petiole, not of each leaflet.
So a leaflet has no axillary bud.
example.answer: A leaflet has no bud in its axil; a simple leaf does.

learn.reallife: Neem twigs used as datun in Indian villages carry pinnately compound leaves; the silk cotton (semal) tree that lights up in red in spring has palmately compound leaves.

games.title: Compound leaf check
items: Neem has a pinnately compound leaf.
Silk cotton has a palmately compound leaf.
Leaflets arise at the petiole tip.
Each leaflet of a compound leaf has a bud in its axil.
Only the petiole axil has a bud.
In a simple leaf, incisions may reach the midrib.
If they reach the midrib, the leaf is compound.
It is the common axis of a pinnate leaf.

quiz.q: Neem has which type of leaf?
quiz.explain: Neem leaflets are on a common rachis.

quiz.q: In a palmately compound leaf, leaflets are attached:
quiz.explain: Palmate leaflets radiate from the petiole tip, as in silk cotton.
options: At a common point at the tip of the petiole

quiz.q: Guava shows which phyllotaxy?
quiz.explain: Guava and Calotropis have a pair of leaves at each node.

quiz.q: Alstonia shows:
quiz.explain: More than two leaves arise at each node of Alstonia.
quiz.mistake: Picks opposite because of the pairing

quiz.q: A leaf is compound when:
quiz.explain: Incisions reaching the midrib break the lamina into leaflets.
options: Incisions of the lamina reach the midrib, forming leaflets

quiz.q: Phyllotaxy refers to:
quiz.explain: Phyllotaxy is leaf arrangement; venation is vein arrangement.
options: The arrangement of leaves on a stem

quiz.q: China rose shows which phyllotaxy?
quiz.explain: A single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A leaflet of a compound leaf has no axillary bud. Reason (R): In a compound leaf, the axillary bud is found only in the axil of the petiole.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R explains why the leaflets themselves lack buds.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu thinks each neem leaflet is a separate leaf. Correct him and explain phyllotaxy too!
teach.praise: Chirp! Find the bud to find the leaf! And leaves can be alternate, opposite or whorled.
teach.nudge: Good! How do you tell a leaflet from a leaf, and what are the three phyllotaxy types?

learn.hook: On a mustard spike in a Rajasthan field, the youngest buds are at the top. On some other plants, the oldest flower sits at the tip. The axis decides.
points: A flower is a modified shoot: the shoot apical meristem becomes a floral meristem, internodes do not elongate, the axis condenses, and floral appendages form at successive nodes instead of leaves.
When the shoot tip itself becomes a flower, the flower is solitary. The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is the inflorescence.
Racemose: the main axis continues to grow, and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession (older flowers at the base, younger towards the tip).
Cymose: the main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is limited; flowers are borne in basipetal order (older at the tip, younger below).
Quick test: if the apex keeps growing, it is racemose; if the apex has become a flower, it is cymose.

example.q: On an inflorescence, the topmost flower opened first and the lower ones later. Which type is it?
steps: The terminal flower is the oldest, so the axis ended in a flower.
Older flowers above, younger below means basipetal order.

learn.reallife: Mustard fields of Punjab and Rajasthan in winter show racemose inflorescences, with buds still opening near the tip as the axis grows.

games.title: Inflorescence check
items: A flower is a modified shoot.
The shoot apical meristem becomes a floral meristem.
In racemose inflorescence, the youngest flowers are near the base.
In cymose inflorescence, growth of the main axis is limited.
A solitary flower forms when the shoot tip turns into a flower.
In basipetal order, older flowers are at the top.
Internodes of a floral axis elongate a lot.
They do not elongate, and the axis condenses.

quiz.q: In a racemose inflorescence, the flowers are arranged in:
quiz.explain: Older flowers below, younger above: acropetal.

quiz.q: In a cymose inflorescence, the main axis:
quiz.explain: The apex becomes a flower, limiting growth.

quiz.q: The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is called:
quiz.explain: Inflorescence is the arrangement of flowers.

quiz.q: A flower is regarded as a modified:
quiz.explain: The shoot apical meristem changes into a floral meristem.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a flower is a modified leaf

quiz.q: Basipetal order means:
quiz.explain: Basipetal is typical of cymose inflorescences.
options: All flowers of the same age
Older flowers at the top, younger towards the base
Older flowers at the base, younger at the top

quiz.q: Which is the key difference between racemose and cymose inflorescences?
quiz.explain: Racemose axes keep growing; cymose axes end in a flower.
options: Whether the main axis continues to grow or ends in a flower

quiz.q: When a flower is formed, the internodes of the floral axis:
quiz.explain: Condensed internodes allow floral whorls to form close together.
options: Do not elongate, so the axis condenses

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Growth of the main axis is limited in a racemose inflorescence. Reason (R): In a racemose inflorescence, the apex does not turn into a flower.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: in racemose inflorescence the main axis keeps growing; limited growth is a cymose feature. R is true: the apex never becomes a flower, which is why growth is unlimited.
quiz.mistake: Judges the assertion true just because the reason is a correct fact

teach.ask: Gappu sees flowers at different heights on a stalk. Teach him racemose vs cymose inflorescence!
teach.praise: Tweet! Axis keeps growing: racemose. Axis ends in a flower: cymose!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the main axis in each type, and how are the flowers ordered?

topics.title: The flower: whorls, sex and symmetry

learn.hook: Cut a datura flower in any direction through the centre and you get two equal halves. Try that with a pea flower and only one cut works.
points: The flower is the reproductive unit of angiosperms. Its four whorls sit on the swollen end of the pedicel, the thalamus (receptacle): calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx and corolla are accessory organs; androecium and gynoecium are reproductive organs. When calyx and corolla are not distinct, as in lily, they are called perianth.
Bisexual flower: has both androecium and gynoecium. Unisexual flower: has only stamens or only carpels.

Symmetry: actinomorphic (radial) if any radial plane through the centre gives two equal halves (mustard, datura, chilli); zygomorphic (bilateral) if only one vertical plane does (pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia); asymmetric if none does (canna).

Trimerous, tetramerous and pentamerous flowers have floral parts in multiples of 3, 4 and 5. Flowers with bracts (reduced leaves at the base of the pedicel) are bracteate; those without are ebracteate.

example.q: A flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 5 stamens and can be cut into two equal halves along any radial plane. Describe it.
steps: Parts in multiples of five: pentamerous.
Equal halves in any radial plane: actinomorphic.

learn.reallife: Chilli flowers in Andhra Pradesh's Guntur district, India's chilli capital, are small, white and actinomorphic.

games.title: Term to meaning
pairs: Reduced leaf at the base of the pedicel

quiz.q: The swollen end of the pedicel on which floral whorls are borne is the:
quiz.explain: The thalamus (receptacle) carries all four whorls.

quiz.q: A flower that can be divided into two similar halves only in one vertical plane is:
quiz.explain: Pea and gulmohur flowers are zygomorphic.

quiz.q: Canna has which type of flower symmetry?
quiz.explain: No vertical plane divides a canna flower into similar halves.

quiz.q: When calyx and corolla cannot be told apart, as in lily, they are called:
quiz.explain: The undifferentiated outer whorls form the perianth.

quiz.q: Which are the reproductive whorls of a flower?
quiz.explain: Stamens and carpels are reproductive; sepals and petals are accessory.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up accessory and reproductive whorls

quiz.q: A flower with floral parts in multiples of four is:
quiz.explain: Tetra- means four.

quiz.q: A flower lacking bracts is described as:
quiz.explain: Ebracteate means without bracts.
quiz.mistake: Confuses bracts with sex of the flower

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A unisexual flower has only stamens or only carpels. Reason (R): In a unisexual flower, the calyx and corolla are always absent.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is the definition of unisexual. R is false: unisexual flowers can have sepals and petals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks unisexual flowers lack all accessory whorls

teach.ask: Gappu holds a datura flower and a pea flower. Explain the parts of a flower and the types of symmetry!
teach.praise: Chirp! Four whorls on a thalamus; datura is actinomorphic, pea is zygomorphic. Bloom-tastic!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the four whorls, and how do the symmetry types differ?

topics.title: Position of ovary, calyx and corolla aestivation

learn.hook: Look at a guava fruit: the dried flower parts sit on its top. That tells you the ovary was 'inferior', sunk inside the thalamus.
points: Hypogynous: gynoecium highest, other parts below it; ovary superior (mustard, china rose, brinjal). Perigynous: gynoecium in the centre, other parts on the rim of the thalamus at about the same level; ovary half-inferior (plum, rose, peach). Epigynous: thalamus grows up and fuses with the ovary, other parts arise above it; ovary inferior (guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower).
Calyx: outermost whorl of sepals, usually green and leaf-like, protecting the bud. Gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (free).
Corolla: petals, usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination; gamopetalous or polypetalous. Shapes include tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped and wheel-shaped.

Aestivation is the arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud relative to others in the same whorl. Valvate: margins just touch, no overlap (Calotropis). Twisted: each margin overlaps the next in one direction (china rose, lady's finger, cotton). Imbricate: margins overlap in no particular direction (Cassia, gulmohur).
Vexillary (papilionaceous) in pea and bean: the largest petal (standard) overlaps two lateral wings, which overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel).

example.q: In a pea flower, which petal is outermost in the bud and which is innermost?
steps: Vexillary aestivation has five petals.
The large standard overlaps the two wings.
The wings overlap the two keel petals.
example.answer: Standard is outermost; keel is innermost.

learn.reallife: Cotton and bhindi (lady's finger), both major crops in Gujarat and Maharashtra, show twisted aestivation in their petals.

quiz.q: In which flower is the ovary inferior?
quiz.explain: Guava is epigynous with an inferior ovary.

quiz.q: Perigynous flowers have an ovary that is:
quiz.explain: Other parts are on the thalamus rim at about the ovary's level.

quiz.q: Twisted aestivation is found in:
quiz.explain: Each petal overlaps the next in one direction.
options: China rose, lady's finger and cotton

quiz.q: In valvate aestivation, the sepals or petals:
quiz.explain: Valvate means edge-to-edge contact, as in Calotropis.
options: Just touch at the margins without overlapping

quiz.q: In vexillary aestivation, the two smallest anterior petals are called the:
quiz.explain: Standard is largest, wings are lateral, keel is smallest and anterior.

quiz.q: A calyx with united sepals is:
quiz.explain: Gamo- means united.

quiz.q: Brinjal flowers are:
quiz.explain: Brinjal has a superior ovary.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Petals are usually brightly coloured. Reason (R): Bright petals attract insects for pollination.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; attracting pollinators is the reason for bright colours.

teach.ask: Gappu sees a guava with flower remains on top. Explain ovary position and the types of aestivation!
teach.praise: Tweet! Superior, half-inferior, inferior, and four kinds of petal folding. Floral origami!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the three ovary positions, and how do valvate and twisted aestivation differ?

learn.hook: In a hibiscus flower, the stamens form a single tube around the style. In a pea, nine join and one stays apart. Stamens love teamwork in different ways.
points: The androecium is made of stamens, the male reproductive organs. Each stamen has a stalk (filament) and an anther.
An anther is usually bilobed, and each lobe has two chambers, the pollen sacs, where pollen grains form. A sterile stamen is a staminode.
Epipetalous stamens are attached to petals (brinjal). Epiphyllous stamens are attached to the perianth (lily).
Stamens may be free (polyandrous) or united: monoadelphous (one bundle, china rose), diadelphous (two bundles, pea), polyadelphous (more than two bundles, citrus).
Filament length may vary within a flower, as in Salvia and mustard.

example.q: How many pollen sacs does a typical stamen have?
steps: A typical anther is bilobed: 2 lobes.
Each lobe has 2 chambers (pollen sacs).
Total = 2 × 2 = 4.

learn.reallife: Lemon and orange orchards of Nagpur grow citrus flowers with polyadelphous stamens in several bundles.

games.title: Stamen facts
items: A staminode is a sterile stamen.
Each anther lobe has two pollen sacs.
A typical bilobed anther has four pollen sacs.
Diadelphous stamens are united in one bundle.
Epipetalous stamens are attached to petals.
Mustard has filaments of different lengths.
Filament length varies within the flower.
A stamen consists of stigma and style.
It consists of filament and anther.

quiz.q: A stamen consists of:
quiz.explain: Filament is the stalk; the anther makes pollen.
quiz.mistake: Gives the parts of a carpel

quiz.q: A sterile stamen is called a:
quiz.explain: Staminode is a stamen that does not produce fertile pollen.

quiz.q: Stamens united in two bundles are:
quiz.explain: Di- means two, as in pea.

quiz.q: Stamens attached to the perianth, as in lily, are:
quiz.explain: Epiphyllous means on the perianth.

quiz.q: How many pollen sacs are present in a typical bilobed anther?
quiz.explain: Two lobes, each with two pollen sacs: 2 × 2 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Counts lobes instead of pollen sacs
steps: Lobes = 2
Pollen sacs per lobe = 2

quiz.q: China rose has which type of stamens?
quiz.explain: All stamens of china rose are united in one bundle around the style.

quiz.q: Citrus has stamens that are:
quiz.explain: Citrus stamens form more than two bundles.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Brinjal has epipetalous stamens. Reason (R): In brinjal, stamens are fused with the gynoecium.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Brinjal stamens are attached to the petals (A true). R is false: they are not fused with the gynoecium.
quiz.mistake: Confuses epipetalous with fusion to the carpel

teach.ask: Gappu sees stamens in a hibiscus forming a tube. Explain the parts of a stamen and how stamens can be joined!
teach.praise: Chirp! Filament plus anther, and stamens can bundle up in one, two or many groups!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the parts of a stamen, and what do monoadelphous and diadelphous mean?

learn.hook: Slice a tomato across and you see seeds attached to a central axis in separate chambers. Slice a pea pod and they sit along one edge. That's placentation.
points: The gynoecium is the female reproductive part, made of one or more carpels. Each carpel has a stigma (receptive surface for pollen), style (connects stigma to ovary) and ovary (enlarged base).
Ovules are attached to a flattened, cushion-like placenta in the ovary. After fertilisation ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Apocarpous: carpels free (lotus, rose). Syncarpous: carpels fused (mustard, tomato).

Placentation types: marginal (ridge along the ventral suture, two rows of ovules; pea), axile (central axis in a multilocular ovary; china rose, tomato, lemon), parietal (ovules on the inner wall; one-chambered ovary made two-chambered by a false septum; mustard, Argemone).
Free central: ovules on a central axis with no septa (Dianthus, Primrose). Basal: placenta at the base with a single ovule (sunflower, marigold).

example.q: A lemon cut crosswise shows several chambers with seeds attached at the centre. Name the placentation.
steps: Multilocular ovary.
Ovules attached to a central axis.
This is axile placentation.

learn.reallife: Marigold flowers, used in lakhs of garlands during Diwali, have basal placentation with a single ovule.

quiz.q: Placentation in pea is:
quiz.explain: Ovules lie in two rows on a ridge along the ventral suture.

quiz.q: Axile placentation is found in:
quiz.explain: Ovules are on a central axis in a multilocular ovary.

quiz.q: In which placentation does a false septum make a one-chambered ovary two-chambered?
quiz.explain: Mustard and Argemone show parietal placentation with a false septum.

quiz.q: Free central placentation is seen in:
quiz.explain: Ovules are on a central axis without septa.

quiz.q: A gynoecium with free carpels is called:
quiz.explain: Lotus and rose have free carpels.

quiz.q: The receptive surface for pollen grains is the:
quiz.explain: Pollen lands on the stigma.

quiz.q: In sunflower and marigold, placentation is:
quiz.explain: The placenta is at the base with a single ovule.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A ripened ovary forms the fruit. Reason (R): After fertilisation, ovules develop into seeds.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true statements about events after fertilisation, but seed formation from ovules does not explain how the ovary becomes the fruit.
quiz.mistake: Links two parallel facts as cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu cuts open a tomato, a pea pod and a mustard fruit. Explain carpels and placentation using them!
teach.praise: Tweet! Stigma, style, ovary, and seeds placed in five different ways. Tomato science!
teach.nudge: Good! What is placentation, and what type is seen in tomato and pea?

topics.title: Fruit and the parts of a seed

learn.hook: In a mango, you eat the middle layer and throw away the hard inner one. In a coconut, the middle layer becomes coir ropes.
points: A fruit is a mature or ripened ovary that develops after fertilisation; it is a characteristic feature of flowering plants. A fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic.
A fruit has a wall (pericarp) and seeds. A thick, fleshy pericarp is differentiated into an outer epicarp, middle mesocarp and inner endocarp.
Mango and coconut fruits are drupes: they develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded.
In mango, the epicarp is thin, the mesocarp is fleshy and edible, and the endocarp is stony and hard. In coconut, the mesocarp is fibrous.
A seed develops from a fertilised ovule. It has a seed coat and an embryo; the embryo has a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (wheat, maize) or two (gram, pea) cotyledons.

example.q: Which layer of a mango do we eat, and which forms the hard 'guthli' shell?
steps: Mango is a drupe with epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp.
The fleshy edible part is the mesocarp.
The stony layer around the seed is the endocarp.
example.answer: We eat the mesocarp; the hard shell is the endocarp.

learn.reallife: Kerala's coir industry turns the fibrous mesocarp of coconut into ropes and mats; seedless banana and grapes are parthenocarpic varieties sold in Indian markets.

games.title: Fruit and seed facts
items: A fruit is a ripened ovary.
One-seeded, from a monocarpellary superior ovary.
The mesocarp of coconut is fleshy and edible.
The ovary forms the fruit; ovules form seeds.
Maize is a monocot with one cotyledon.

quiz.q: A fruit that develops without fertilisation is called:
quiz.explain: Parthenocarpy means fruit formation without fertilisation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a fruit type with its mode of formation

quiz.q: The edible part of mango is the:
quiz.explain: The fleshy mesocarp is eaten.

quiz.q: In coconut, the mesocarp is:
quiz.explain: The fibrous mesocarp gives coir.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all drupes have a fleshy mesocarp

quiz.q: Drupes develop from:
quiz.explain: Mango and coconut are one-seeded drupes from monocarpellary superior ovaries.
options: Monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded
Multicarpellary inferior ovaries with many seeds

quiz.q: The three layers of a fleshy pericarp, from outside, are:
quiz.explain: Epi = outer, meso = middle, endo = inner.

quiz.q: A seed is made up of:
quiz.explain: The embryo inside has a radicle, embryonal axis and cotyledons.
options: A seed coat and an embryo

quiz.q: Which plants have embryos with two cotyledons?
quiz.explain: Gram and pea are dicots.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mango is called a drupe. Reason (R): Mango develops from a monocarpellary superior ovary and has a single seed with a stony endocarp.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R lists the features that define a drupe.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that R defines a drupe

teach.ask: Gappu is eating a mango and wonders what each layer is. Explain fruits, the pericarp and what's inside a seed!
teach.praise: Chirp! Skin, flesh and stone are epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp. My mango is a drupe!
teach.nudge: Good! What is a fruit, and what are the three layers of a mango?

topics.title: Structure of dicot and monocot seeds

learn.hook: Soak a gram seed overnight and it splits into two fat halves. A maize grain refuses to split. Their insides are built differently.
points: Dicot seed: the seed coat has an outer testa and inner tegmen. The hilum is the scar where the seed was attached to the fruit; the micropyle is a small pore above the hilum.
The dicot embryo has an embryonal axis with a radicle and plumule at its ends, and two cotyledons that are often fleshy and full of food.
Endospermic seeds keep the endosperm (formed by double fertilisation) as food-storing tissue, e.g. castor. Non-endospermic seeds have no endosperm in the mature seed, e.g. bean, gram, pea.

Monocot seeds are generally endospermic (orchids are non-endospermic). In maize, the seed coat is membranous and fused with the fruit wall; the bulky endosperm is separated from the embryo by a proteinous aleurone layer.

The maize embryo lies in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It has one large, shield-shaped cotyledon, the scutellum, and a short axis with plumule and radicle enclosed in sheaths, the coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively.

example.q: Name the sheaths that cover the plumule and the radicle in a maize embryo.
steps: The plumule is the future shoot; its sheath is the coleoptile.
The radicle is the future root; its sheath is the coleorhiza.
example.answer: Coleoptile covers the plumule; coleorhiza covers the radicle.

learn.reallife: India's maize belt in Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh grows corn whose grains are endospermic; soaked chana (gram) sprouts show two cotyledons and no endosperm.

games.title: Seed part to description
pairs: Outer layer of the seed coat
Scar of attachment to the fruit

quiz.q: The scar on a seed coat where the seed was attached to the fruit is the:
quiz.explain: The hilum marks the point of attachment.

quiz.q: Which is an endospermic dicot seed?
quiz.explain: Castor keeps its endosperm; gram, pea and bean do not.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all dicot seeds are non-endospermic

quiz.q: The single shield-shaped cotyledon of maize is the:
quiz.explain: Scutellum is the maize cotyledon.

quiz.q: The coleoptile encloses the:
quiz.explain: Coleoptile covers the plumule; coleorhiza covers the radicle.

quiz.q: The proteinous layer separating the endosperm from the embryo in maize is the:
quiz.explain: The aleurone layer is the outer covering of the endosperm.

quiz.q: The inner layer of the dicot seed coat is the:
quiz.explain: Outer testa, inner tegmen.

quiz.q: Which monocot seeds are non-endospermic?
quiz.explain: Most monocot seeds are endospermic; orchids are an exception.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In maize, the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall. Reason (R): In maize, the seed coat is membranous.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true features of maize grain, but being membranous does not explain why the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall.
quiz.mistake: Thinks two true descriptions must be cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu soaks chana and maize. 'Why does chana split in two but maize doesn't?' Compare dicot and monocot seeds!
teach.praise: Tweet! Two cotyledons in chana, one scutellum plus endosperm in maize. Seed secrets revealed!
teach.nudge: Good! How many cotyledons does each have, and where is the food stored in maize?

topics.title: Semi-technical description, floral formula and floral diagram

learn.hook: A floral formula is like a cricket scorecard: a single line tells you everything about a flower if you know the symbols.
points: A semi-technical description uses brief, scientific language in a set sequence: habit, then vegetative characters (root, stem, leaves), then floral characters (inflorescence and flower parts), followed by the floral diagram and floral formula.
Symbols: Br bracteate, K calyx, C corolla, P perianth, A androecium, G gynoecium; ♂ male, ♀ female, ⚥ bisexual; ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic.
A line below G (G̲) shows a superior ovary; a line above G (Ḡ) shows an inferior ovary. Numbers give the count of parts.

Fusion (cohesion) of members of a whorl is shown by putting the number in brackets, e.g. C(5) means five united petals. Adhesion between whorls is shown by a line drawn above the symbols of those whorls, e.g. joining C and A for epipetalous stamens.

Floral diagram: a dot at the top shows the position of the mother axis. Calyx (outermost), corolla, androecium and gynoecium (centre) are drawn as successive whorls, showing number, aestivation, cohesion, adhesion and placentation. The NCERT example is mustard (family Brassicaceae).

example.q: Decode: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), with a line joining C and A, and G(2) underlined.
steps: ⊕ actinomorphic, ⚥ bisexual.
K(5): five united sepals; C(5): five united petals.
A5 joined to C by a line: five epipetalous stamens.
G(2) underlined: bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary.
example.answer: An actinomorphic bisexual flower with 5 united sepals, 5 united petals, 5 epipetalous stamens and a bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary.

learn.reallife: Botanists at the Botanical Survey of India write floral formulae in field notebooks to record new plants quickly, much like a scorer's shorthand at a Ranji Trophy match.

games.title: Order of a semi-technical description
games.prompt: Put the sections in the order they are written

quiz.q: In a floral formula, C(5) means:
quiz.explain: Brackets show cohesion (fusion) within a whorl.

quiz.q: The symbol % in a floral formula stands for:
quiz.explain: % shows a zygomorphic flower; ⊕ is actinomorphic.

quiz.q: A line drawn below G in a floral formula indicates:
quiz.explain: G̲ means superior; Ḡ means inferior.

quiz.q: In a floral diagram, the dot at the top represents the:
quiz.explain: The dot shows the position of the mother axis relative to the flower.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the dot is a floral part

quiz.q: Adhesion between two whorls in a floral formula is shown by:
quiz.explain: A line above the symbols joins the adhering whorls, e.g. C and A.
options: A line drawn above the symbols of those whorls

quiz.q: In a floral diagram, which whorl is drawn at the centre?
quiz.explain: Calyx is outermost; gynoecium is in the centre.
quiz.mistake: Places the calyx at the centre

quiz.q: In a semi-technical description, which is described first?
quiz.explain: Description starts with habit, then vegetative and floral characters.

quiz.q: In the formula ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), how many floral parts (sepals + petals + stamens) are there outside the gynoecium?
quiz.explain: Sepals 5 + petals 5 + stamens 5 = 15.
quiz.mistake: Adds the carpels or misses a whorl
steps: K(5) → 5 sepals
C(5) → 5 petals
A5 → 5 stamens

teach.ask: Gappu sees '⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2)' and thinks it's a secret code. Teach him how to read floral formulae and diagrams!
teach.praise: Chirp! K for calyx, brackets for fusion, a line for adhesion. I can read flowers now!
teach.nudge: Good! What do the brackets and the line under G mean?

learn.hook: Your aloo paratha, tomato chutney, baingan bharta and green chilli all come from one plant family. Meet Solanaceae.
points: Solanaceae (potato family) is a large family spread across tropics, subtropics and temperate zones. Plants are mostly herbs and shrubs, rarely small trees.

Stem: herbaceous, rarely woody; erect, cylindrical, branched, solid or hollow, hairy or glabrous; underground stem in potato (Solanum tuberosum). Leaves: alternate, simple, rarely pinnately compound, exstipulate, reticulate venation.

Floral characters: inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose (as in Solanum); flowers bisexual and actinomorphic. Calyx: five united sepals, persistent, valvate. Corolla: five united petals, valvate. Androecium: five epipetalous stamens.

Gynoecium: bicarpellary, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules; axile placentation. Fruit: berry or capsule. Seeds: many, endospermous. Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), with C and A joined (epipetalous) and G underlined (superior).
Uses: food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco), ornamental (petunia).

example.q: A brinjal flower has 5 united persistent sepals, 5 united petals, 5 stamens attached to petals, and a 2-carpelled fused superior ovary. Write its floral formula.
steps: Actinomorphic and bisexual: ⊕ ⚥.
Sepals united: K(5). Petals united: C(5).
Stamens epipetalous: A5 joined to C(5) by a line.
Two fused carpels, superior: G(2) underlined.
example.answer: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) (C and A joined by a line, G underlined)

learn.reallife: India is among the world's largest producers of potato, tomato and brinjal, and ashwagandha is a major medicinal crop grown in Madhya Pradesh's Mandsaur and Neemuch districts.

games.title: Solanaceae features
items: Five stamens attached to the petals.
The ovary is superior and bilocular.
It is axile with a swollen placenta.
Sepals stay on the fruit, as on a brinjal.

quiz.q: Placentation in Solanaceae is:
quiz.explain: A swollen placenta with many ovules on the axis of a bilocular ovary.

quiz.q: How many stamens does a Solanaceae flower usually have?
quiz.explain: Five epipetalous stamens.

quiz.q: Which Solanaceae plant is used as a medicine?
quiz.explain: Belladonna and ashwagandha are medicinal.
quiz.mistake: Picks a food or ornamental plant

quiz.q: The fruit of Solanaceae is a:
quiz.explain: Fruits are berries (tomato, brinjal) or capsules.

quiz.q: The ovary in Solanaceae is:
quiz.explain: Ovary is superior, made of two fused carpels.

quiz.q: Tobacco is used as a:
quiz.explain: NCERT lists tobacco as a fumigatory.

quiz.q: Aestivation of the calyx and corolla in Solanaceae is:
quiz.explain: Both sepals and petals are valvate.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Potato is placed in Solanaceae. Reason (R): The potato tuber is an underground stem.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but having an underground stem is not why potato belongs to Solanaceae; its floral characters place it there.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a stem feature decides the family

teach.ask: Gappu is shocked that potato, tomato and chilli are 'cousins'. Describe the Solanaceae family to him!
teach.praise: Tweet! One family feeds and heals us. Solanaceae is a superstar!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the floral features of Solanaceae, and name some useful plants?
